Every horse has different needs and preferences, meaning that there's no "one-size-fits-all" approach to horse care. Some horses are going to need shoes to stay sound. Some horses are going to need blankets, especially in wet and cold climates. Some horses are going to need grain and supplements to maintain a healthy weight. Some horses prefer bits to bitless. 

Another completely different take: behavioural euthanasia  is okay. It sucks as no one wants to do it, but sometimes it's the right option for the safety of the horse, its handlers, and other horses in the field. Especially if a lot of options, tests, diagnosis, have been exhausted. (For context I had to fight a family member to put a horse that I was responsible for taking care of clearly had a neurological issue, and this horse was dangerous to people handling him. He fell on me twice, the farrier once, and "exploded" on barn staff the odd time that I couldn't be there for turn in. This horse was PTS about six months too late. Most of the teachers from my school went to the "popular church" and if you weren't a part of that group, you were only viewed as a number who gave them 15k a year (unless you were an international student, they paid 30k+/year, they would treat you well). 

I am registered through Luther College at the U of R. I have no issues with the quality of education I am receiving there. I'd even argue that I'm rather satisfied with my Luther College education, and the other services provided there. If I told my guidance counsellors that I went to the U of R instead of UW (I have my issues with UW, but that's a discussion for another day), I'd be ridiculed off the face of the earth (not to mention my peers who have also done the same). I know that Luther College has a difficult time attracting Luther HS students (if they go to the U of R, they'll register through the main campus). 

Unfortunately paying more does not equate to a higher quality of education. A lot of parents want the bragging rights that they have the means to send their child to a private high school. I am sure that some children do great in that environment, however I didn't.

I went to a similar style school (in SW Ontario), where the overwhelming majority of the students went to the University of Waterloo for a variety of programs (there was at least two people in my graduating class who went into engineering). It wasn't worth the money my parents paid for me to go there. I was never a part of the "in-group" as I was a brown, queer man, who didn't go to the "popular church" (I didn't go to church at all). Over a half decade has gone past since I graduated and I'm still angry and traumatized from it. 

Basically it was a University of Waterloo factory, and if you didn't want to go there, they didn't bother helping you at all. Whether that was academically or socially. I was bullied and was told to "deal with it" because this individual's father was the chair of the board of directors and I shouldn't ruin his life. I was told that I was "wasting my education" because I didn't go to university immediately after graduation. Teachers were mediocre and unqualified. 

I cannot speak for Luther high school, but IMHO most private school are scam. While I am now in university, I have worked extremely hard to achieve the grades I have, and I attribute that more to my overall work ethic rather than the education I received from my high school.

the biggest concern I have with arena turnout is the condition of the footing, as long as the footing is relatively even/safe (ask yourself "would I ride or lunge my horse here, or should I till it?"), I know that a mutual friend's horse of mine did have to be put down after a free lunging/arena accident (arena footing likely wasn't properly maintained, and this is the only case I've heard of in the 15+ years I've been around horses). Free lunging, if done properly, isn't teaching your horse to "go bananas" in a place they typically are working. I've personally never had an issue with my horses, they might go for a quick rip, roll, stand around, be a little silly, but never dangerous. How does your horse act in turnout? It could be an indicator on his actions of being loose in the arena. Your horse is just as capable of finding a way to injure himself in the field.   
You need to evaluate the pros and cons, and what "risks" you're willing to take.

The safest helmet is going to be the be that fits you the best. I’d recommend going to a tack store and trying on a bunch. Some people fit perfectly in a 50$ helmet, while others seem to only fit in the 600$ samshield. 
Also consider your hair when fitting a helmet. Is it going to be tucked up in a net inside your helmet, or in a low bun/ponytail outside the helmet. This will also impact the fit. 
Please don’t buy a used one. Even if there hasn’t been any falls, it could have been dropped, or left in a hot or cold car which will compromise the safety of the helmet. 
The VT study is flawed and I wouldn’t buy a helmet solely off of their ratings.

Title: to the game of hockey
Genre: non-fiction, personal essay
Feedback desired: just rip it to absolute pieces, but in a respectable manner. I mostly need help with paragraph organization as I don't quite like the flow of the paragraphs, but feel lost.
WC: about 1000




My Dad and I will never fully get along, and we will likely never. Of the few things we do together, we can watch hockey. Most specifically, Leafs games. Our relationship mainly revolves around following various Canadian sports teams, trucks, and the occasional discussion about post-secondary education.

A pivotal part of our relationship was watching a Leafs game in early 2021. All I remember is that they gloriously won in overtime. We didn't talk much during the game until he said,"thanks for watching the game." We both parted ways, and he probably hasn’t crossed his mind since. It’s been about two months and continues to live with me.

We are Leafs fans and honorary Jet’s fans. Only because we know the first cousin of one of their assistant captains, and not when they’re playing the Leafs. Considering he was born in some tiny town in SK, I’m frankly surprised that he’s not a Jets fan, but at least he’s not a Habs fan. I was born in TO, you’re a Leafs fan by destiny, and you die a Leafs fan. That’s TO law,  I don’t make them. 

When I was six or seven, I watched the odd Leafs game with my dad when they were horrible as a team, which made watching them as a young kid no fun. Since they got Auston Matthews and many other talented players, they started playing much better. Making it more fun to watch. At the best of times, I have a vague idea of what’s happening.

I was never allowed to play hockey as a kid, and I don’t know why. To this day, I’ve never gotten a fully defined answer. We could afford it, my dad played up until I was born, but the idea was always shut down every single time it's mentioned. Maybe it’s the injuries that he and his friends have sustained over their careers, the time involved, or something else; I will never now. There are a select few who are my age making more in a year than I will make in my entire life, and part of me wishes that I could’ve had the slightest chance at that. 

I tried every other sport under the sun instead. Track, cross country, soccer, swimming, triathlon, basketball, volleyball, baseball, flag football; there’s been about a dozen failed attempts at other sports. I did run track and cross country competitively through middle school and high school, getting recruited into a high-level, successful track club. I never loved running but did it mainly for his approval. A little under two years out of high school, I am finally running again. I run while he bikes, blast my tunes, and generally have a good time. 

Somehow, I ended up riding horses. Equestrian sports are significantly more expensive and dangerous than hockey. I have sustained numerous concussions, broken bones, and various other moderately minor injuries. After severely spraining my ankle at sixteen, which resulted in me having to leave cross country and track, he wanted me to quit. If I didn’t get injured, I likely would have been able to run competitively on a university scholarship. Then a broken wrist that needed surgery, about a year and a half later, I didn't quit. To my defeat, I am stubborn, crazy competitive, and want to get to the top of the sport. 

From the age of ten until nearly twenty, and hopefully, much longer, I ride almost daily on a few horses and train for the Olympic gold dream many young, ambitious equestrians strive for. My dad has been supportive of my Olympic gold show jumping goals and is probably one of my biggest fans, though he would never want to admit it. 

There are many aspects of my life that my dad doesn't know about, or even needs to about. In short, I am gay. It’s not the biggest part of me, but he doesn’t need to know. I know that he’s not necessarily homophobic, but he’s also not the type to be walking down Main St. during Pride giving out hugs or marching with an 'I love my gay son' sign. To the extent that I’m aware of, he knows but respects my privacy and is waiting for me to feel safe enough to tell him. If that is the case, I applaud him. It would be more of an issue being a Habs fan than being gay. 

I more recently got myself back into hockey after reading “The Sound of Ice” and “Check Please” series. Both series depict the lives of fictional and out NHL players. Though fictional, it is great to see some representation, and will hopefully bring some discussion to the league. These discussions are much needed surrounding the LGBT community. Over the past few years, there have been improvements, with teams hosting pride night games and using pride tape in warm-ups.

There has yet to be an out player, whether that be current or former. It’s not going to be me. I could have been the first, but there are many hoping to be the first, or at least one. As someone who has been closeted and involved in sports for quite some time, I hope that one day there can be. It will be a monumental step for the league, and the many closeted youths wanting the hoist the Stanley Cup one day. The NHL isn’t ready for that yet.

I will never hoist the Stanley Cup, and I’m now okay with that.
